screens.title: Plan Azure Database Deployments: Service Tiers & Networking
screens.narratorSegment: Before provisioning any database in Azure, effective planning sets the stage for reliability, cost control, and operational simplicity. In this lesson you will learn how to decide between Platform as a Service and Infrastructure as a Service, how service tiers like General Purpose, Business Critical and Hyperscale affect performance and resilience, and how compute models such as vCore or DTU change scaling and billing. You will also learn networking fundamentals that keep your data private — Virtual Networks, subnets, and Private Endpoints — and why those choices matter for compliance and latency. For example, selecting a Flexible Server for PostgreSQL can give you VNet integration and zone-redundant availability, while choosing a Managed Instance often simplifies lift-and-shift migrations because of near 100% S Q L Server compatibility. A common misconception is that PaaS always costs more; in many cases the reduced operational overhead and built-in HA lower total cost of ownership. As you proceed, notice the three core topics below — service model, tier & compute, and secure networking — and think about which trade-offs matter most for your application requirements.

Plan Azure Database Deployments: Service Tiers & Networking
Choose the service model and network controls that match workload needs for performance, security, and budget.
In this lesson
You will compare PaaS and IaaS, map service tiers to workload types, and plan VNets, private endpoints, and cost controls.
Why it matters
A correct service and network choice reduces downtime, improves compliance, and prevents unexpected bills during scale events.
Explore Key Topics
Service Models
PaaS vs IaaS trade-offs for operations and control.
Tiers & Compute
General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale, vCore and DTU choices.
Networking
VNets, Private Endpoints, and service endpoints for secure access.
Concept Map
PaaS: Managed
Managed engine, built-in HA, less operational overhead.
IaaS: Full control
Full OS and engine control, more management work.
Quick example
A new web app needing moderate throughput, budget constraints, and private VNet-only access is often best served by an Azure SQL Database in General Purpose with a Private Endpoint.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the planning work you'll do for Azure database deployments. First, you will evaluate when to choose PaaS versus IaaS by weighing operational responsibilities, compatibility requirements, and control over the OS and database engine. For example, if you need near-100% S Q L Server feature compatibility, Managed Instance may be the right choice. Second, you'll learn the available service tiers and compute models for Azure S Q L Database and the managed open-source offerings, and be able to match General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale, or Flexible Server options to workload profiles. Third, you will identify and configure core networking elements — Virtual Networks, subnets, Private Endpoints and service endpoints — so your database traffic stays private and compliant. Finally, you will analyze cost implications across tiers and compute choices, and apply options such as reserved instances or license benefits to optimize spend. Each objective combines a practical skill and a reason why that skill reduces risk or cost in production deployments.

screens.title: PaaS vs IaaS: Choosing the right service model
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Platform as a Service and Infrastructure as a Service is a foundational planning decision. Platform as a Service, which includes Azure S Q L Database, Managed Instance, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL, hands off operating system management, patching, and much of the high availability work to the provider. This reduces operational burden and accelerates application delivery. In contrast, Infrastructure as a Service — a database running on an Azure Virtual Machine — gives you control over the OS, exact S Q L Server version, and all S Q L configuration, but that control comes with responsibility for patching, backups, and implementing high availability. A common concrete example: if you have legacy S Q L Agent jobs or cross-database queries that depend on specific S Q L Server features, IaaS or Managed Instance may be required because Azure S Q L Database may not expose every on-premises feature. A typical misconception is to assume PaaS means loss of control; instead, PaaS trades low-level control for managed capability, often improving reliability and reducing cost of operations. When deciding, list requirements for feature compatibility, control over OS, and acceptable operational overhead. Ask: do I need full engine control, or will managed platform features and built-in HA outweigh the benefits of control?

keyIdea.text: PaaS reduces operational burden; IaaS gives full control — choose based on compatibility needs and management capacity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › PaaS vs IaaS
Comparison: Responsibilities
PaaS (Azure SQL, Managed Instance, Flexible Server)
  • Provider manages OS, patching, and many HA features.
  • Focus shifts to schema, queries, and security configuration.
IaaS (SQL on VM)
  • You manage OS, backups, patching, and HA design.
  • Useful when exact engine control or unsupported features are required.
Concrete example
If your application relies on SQL Agent jobs or cross-database ownership chaining that requires specific SQL Server editions, Managed Instance or a VM gives the compatibility you need; pure Azure SQL Database might not.
Decision checklist
  1. Inventory required SQL features and OS-level controls.
  2. Estimate operational capacity for patching and HA maintenance.
  3. Match feature needs to PaaS options or choose IaaS when control is mandatory.
Key Takeaway

Choose PaaS for reduced operations and built-in resilience; choose IaaS when engine-level control and custom OS configs are non-negotiable.

Common mistake
Assuming PaaS always increases cost. Often operational savings and built-in HA offset higher list prices.

screens.title: Azure SQL Database Service Tiers
screens.narratorSegment: Azure S Q L Database exposes distinct service tiers to fit varying workload needs. General Purpose is intended for most business workloads; it balances performance and cost by decoupling compute and storage so you can scale resources independently. Business Critical is for input and output-intensive or mission-critical applications: it uses local SSD storage and multiple replicas to provide higher resilience and lower read latency. Hyperscale is an architecture that separates compute from storage differently and can scale to support very large databases by expanding storage independently and adding rapid scale-out techniques, making it suitable for massive OLTP scenarios. Each tier impacts latency, failover behavior, and cost. For instance, an OLTP workload with frequent small transactions might benefit from Business Critical for its local SSD performance, while an analytics-heavy or very large transactional dataset may require Hyperscale for growth beyond traditional limits. A common misconception is that higher tiers always fix application-level bottlenecks; tier selection addresses infrastructure capability, but poorly optimized queries or indexes will still limit performance. When choosing a tier, profile your workload's input and output patterns, size growth expectations, and tolerance for failover behavior, then map those needs to the tier characteristics.

keyIdea.title: Tier mapping
keyIdea.text: Pick General Purpose for balanced workloads, Business Critical for I/O demand, and Hyperscale for massive growth and scale.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Azure SQL Database Tiers
Tier cards
General Purpose
Balanced performance and cost with decoupled compute and storage; good default for many business apps.
Business Critical
Highest resilience and I/O performance using local SSDs and replicas for mission-critical workloads.
Hyperscale
Independent compute and storage scaling for very large databases and rapid growth scenarios.
Key Takeaway

Match tier to I/O pattern and growth needs; higher tiers improve infrastructure capabilities but not application design.

How to choose — quick workflow
  1. Profile your workload I/O and size requirements over expected growth.
  2. Decide if local SSD performance or multiple replicas are required.
  3. Choose General Purpose, Business Critical, or Hyperscale accordingly and validate with a test workload.
Misconception check
Higher tier does not eliminate inefficient schema or queries. Always profile and optimize application-level bottlenecks first.

screens.title: Compute models: vCore, DTU, and serverless
screens.narratorSegment: Compute models determine how you size and pay for database resources. The vCore model exposes C P U and memory directly, allowing granular scaling of vCores and offering a provisioned or serverless option in some services. Provisioned vCores charge for allocated capacity regardless of use; this is predictable and useful for steady, high-utilization workloads. Serverless vCore lets compute scale with demand and can pause during inactivity to reduce cost, which is helpful for bursty or sporadic workloads. The DTU model, by contrast, packs compute, memory, and input and output into a single unit which simplifies sizing but reduces granularity. A concrete example: choosing provisioned vCores for a database with 24/7 steady traffic avoids repeated scaling events and gives predictable performance, while serverless may save money for a dev/test database that is idle many hours per day. The common misconception is that serverless always saves money; if a workload stays busy or requires consistent performance, serverless may be more expensive. When planning, compare usage patterns, the need for predictable latency, and cost estimates for each model to choose the right approach.

keyIdea.title: Pick compute by workload pattern
keyIdea.text: Use provisioned vCores for steady demand, serverless for intermittent workloads, and DTU for simplified sizing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Compute models
Model comparison
vCore (provisioned)
Granular CPU/memory control; pay for allocated capacity constantly.
vCore (serverless)
Scales compute automatically and can pause when idle to save cost.
DTU
Bundled compute/memory/I/O unit for simplified sizing; less granular control.
Concrete example
A dev database with long idle periods can use serverless to pause compute and save money. A production OLTP service usually uses provisioned vCores for consistent performance.
Checklist for compute selection
  • Measure hourly CPU and I/O usage patterns.
  • Decide if predictable latency or cost savings are the priority.
  • Estimate monthly cost under typical and peak loads for each model.
Misconception
Choosing serverless without analyzing steady-state usage can lead to higher costs and unpredictable latency during scale events.

screens.title: Azure SQL Managed Instance: Compatibility and migration
screens.narratorSegment: Azure S Q L Managed Instance is designed for enterprises looking to lift and shift on-premises S Q L Server workloads to a managed platform while retaining most on-premises features. It offers near 100% compatibility with the latest on-premises S Q L Server, making it a strong choice when migration requires features like S Q L Agent, cross-database queries, or specific configurations that Azure S Q L Database may not support. Managed Instance runs in your Virtual Network, enabling private connectivity that aligns with enterprise network topologies. Use cases include migrating applications with numerous cross-database dependencies or those that rely on OS-level collations and instance-scoped configurations. A common misconception is that Managed Instance removes all operational work; while it relieves you of OS patching and many management tasks, you still need to manage backups, schema migrations, and performance tuning. When planning a migration, inventory features in use, test application behavior against a Managed Instance, and plan VNet sizing and subnet allocation since Managed Instance requires VNet integration. The closing question is: which on-premises features are mandatory for your application, and does Managed Instance meet that compatibility checklist?

keyIdea.title: Migration target
keyIdea.text: Managed Instance is ideal when near-complete SQL Server compatibility is required for lift-and-shift migrations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Managed Instance
Architecture snapshot
Managed Instance runs inside your Virtual Network and provides an instance-scoped environment similar to on-premises SQL Server. It supports features that facilitate lift-and-shift migrations and gives near-complete compatibility with on-premises instances.
Use case
Migrate enterprise apps needing SQL Agent or cross-database queries.
Network
Deploy into a VNet subnet and plan IP space and routing carefully.
Migration checklist
  • Inventory feature use on the source instance.
  • Validate compatibility on a test Managed Instance.
  • Plan VNet address space and subnet size before provisioning.
Concrete example
An app with scheduled SQL Agent jobs and many cross-database queries benefits from Managed Instance because those on-premises features are supported.
Common mistake
Assuming Managed Instance eliminates all migration effort; you still must test jobs, logins, and performance under expected load.

screens.title: Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL: Single Server vs Flexible Server
screens.narratorSegment: When using Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL, you will choose between Single Server and Flexible Server deployment models. Single Server is a fully managed PaaS offering that suits many workloads but has limitations in network isolation and high availability customization. Flexible Server provides more granular control over networking with VNet integration, zone-redundant high availability options, and a more predictable performance model. For production workloads requiring strict network isolation or zone-redundant availability, Flexible Server is the recommended path. A concrete scenario: if your application requires the database to be reachable only within a private VNet and you need zone redundancy, Flexible Server supports VNet integration and zone-redundant deployment, whereas Single Server may leave you constrained. A misconception is to assume Single Server is always simpler for production; while simpler in some respects, its network and HA constraints can make it less suitable for enterprise production needs. When planning, choose Flexible Server for new production deployments and use Single Server for simpler workloads or migration phases where its constraints are acceptable. Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL: Single Server vs Flexible Server means flexible server offers vnet integration and zone-redundant availability, making it preferred for production and strict isolation.. In practical terms, deployment options and networking differences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deployment differences
Single Server
Fully managed but limited VNet isolation and HA customization.
Flexible Server
Offers VNet integration, zone-redundant HA options, and predictable performance behavior.
Concrete example
For a production web app with strict network isolation and high availability across zones, Flexible Server with VNet integration and zone redundancy is the recommended choice.
Decision prompts

screens.title: Compute tiers for open-source managed databases
screens.narratorSegment: For Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL, compute tiers typically include Burstable, General Purpose, and Memory Optimized. Burstable instances are cost-effective for workloads that do not require continuous full C P U — they allow short bursts of C P U usage and are suitable for development, testing, or low-traffic applications. General Purpose balances compute and storage for consistent business applications. Memory Optimized tiers prioritize R A M for workloads with high memory requirements such as large caches or complex joins. A concrete example: a small SaaS tenant with intermittent usage might use a Burstable tier to save cost while a multi-tenant app with heavy joins and in-memory operations might require Memory Optimized. A common misconception is to choose the highest tier to avoid tuning; this is often wasteful. Instead, profile memory and C P U usage, run representative queries, and select a tier matching the dominant resource demand. Also consider storage size and IO characteristics when choosing a tier, because compute alone does not guarantee throughput for input and output-bound workloads. Compute tiers for open-source managed databases means select burstable for intermittent loads, general purpose for balanced needs, memory optimized for ram-heavy workloads.. Tier definitions
Burstable
Cost-effective for intermittent CPU needs; suitable for dev/test and low-traffic services.
General Purpose
Balanced compute and storage for steady business workloads.
Memory Optimized
High RAM for workloads with large in-memory operations or complex queries.
Concrete example
Use Burstable for a staging environment that is idle overnight. Move production, consistent learners to General Purpose or Memory Optimized depending on memory profiles.
Selection checklist
  • Measure peak and sustained CPU usage.
  • Measure working set size to determine memory needs.
  • Balance cost with predictable performance requirements.
Misconception
Assuming compute tier alone fixes slow queries. Optimize schema and queries in addition to picking an appropriate tier.

screens.title: Networking fundamentals: VNets, subnets, and topology
screens.narratorSegment: Networking is essential for securing and isolating database traffic. An Azure Virtual Network provides a logically isolated space with an IP address range and subnets where resources communicate privately. When planning for databases, you must allocate address space and create dedicated subnets for database services, ensuring enough IP addresses for scale and future instances. Also plan routing and Network Security Groups to limit traffic to the required ports and source ranges. Consider how resource groups, peering, and on-premises connectivity will affect topology: for example, will your application servers be in the same VNet, or will you use peering or VPN/ExpressRoute to connect on-premises services? A common pitfall is under-provisioning subnet IP space and later needing disruptive reconfiguration. Always estimate growth and reserve address ranges. For PaaS services that will use Private Endpoints, plan which subnet will host the endpoint and ensure no conflicting network policies. The practical question to end with is: what address space and subnet sizes will you reserve to support current and projected database instances and private endpoints? screens.title: Private Endpoint vs VNet Service Endpoint
screens.narratorSegment: Private Endpoint and VNet Service Endpoint are two options to secure access to Azure PaaS databases, and they behave differently. A Private Endpoint assigns a private IP from your VNet to the PaaS resource, effectively bringing the service into your private network and eliminating public internet exposure. This is the most secure and recommended approach for production workloads. VNet Service Endpoints extend a subnet's identity to the Azure service, allowing you to restrict service access to specific subnets without assigning a private IP to the service. Service Endpoints can be simpler to configure, but they do not remove the service's public endpoint — they only restrict which VNet traffic is allowed. A concrete example: to ensure that only resources inside a specific subnet can reach the database and never allow public access, choose a Private Endpoint. A common misconception is that Service Endpoints provide the same isolation as Private Endpoints; they do not. When planning, prefer Private Endpoints for strict isolation and use Service Endpoints when simpler subnet-level restrictions suffice and private IP assignment is not needed. screens.title: Cost optimization: licensing and instance choices
screens.narratorSegment: Cost optimization should be considered at every planning step. Different service tiers and compute models have distinct pricing behaviors. For example, Business Critical tiers and provisioned vCores typically cost more than General Purpose or serverless because they allocate higher input and output or reserved compute. The Azure Hybrid Benefit is a licensing option that lets you use existing S Q L Server licenses to reduce cost, and reserved instances allow you to commit to one- or three-year terms to get lower prices for predictable workloads. A concrete scenario: if your workload is steady and predictable for enterprise databases, buying reserved capacity and using existing licenses through the Hybrid Benefit reduces ongoing bills. Conversely, if your workload is spiky or development-focused, serverless or Burstable tiers can reduce cost by charging only when resources are used. A misconception is to optimize only list price; instead, consider total cost of ownership including operations, monitoring, and maintenance. The practical exercise is to compare the estimated costs for the same configuration across provisioned vCores, serverless, and DTU models and include licensing benefits and reservations in the analysis.

fullNarratorScript:
Before provisioning any database in Azure, effective planning sets the stage for reliability, cost control, and operational simplicity. In this lesson you will learn how to decide between Platform as a Service and Infrastructure as a Service, how service tiers like General Purpose, Business Critical and Hyperscale affect performance and resilience, and how compute models such as vCore or DTU change scaling and billing. You will also learn networking fundamentals that keep your data private — Virtual Networks, subnets, and Private Endpoints — and why those choices matter for compliance and latency. For example, selecting a Flexible Server for PostgreSQL can give you VNet integration and zone-redundant availability, while choosing a Managed Instance often simplifies lift-and-shift migrations because of near 100% S Q L Server compatibility. A common misconception is that PaaS always costs more; in many cases the reduced operational overhead and built-in HA lower total cost of ownership. As you proceed, notice the three core topics below — service model, tier & compute, and secure networking — and think about which trade-offs matter most for your application requirements.

These objectives guide the planning work you'll do for Azure database deployments. First, you will evaluate when to choose PaaS versus IaaS by weighing operational responsibilities, compatibility requirements, and control over the OS and database engine. For example, if you need near-100% S Q L Server feature compatibility, Managed Instance may be the right choice. Second, you'll learn the available service tiers and compute models for Azure S Q L Database and the managed open-source offerings, and be able to match General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale, or Flexible Server options to workload profiles. Third, you will identify and configure core networking elements — Virtual Networks, subnets, Private Endpoints and service endpoints — so your database traffic stays private and compliant. Finally, you will analyze cost implications across tiers and compute choices, and apply options such as reserved instances or license benefits to optimize spend. Each objective combines a practical skill and a reason why that skill reduces risk or cost in production deployments.

In addition to the high-level goals, these objectives emphasize practical validation steps you will practice. You should be able to identify the appropriate service tier and compute sizing for a given workload profile and simulate the steps to configure a database in the portal without deploying it. You will also be able to design a VNet topology with subnets and place a Private Endpoint into the correct subnet to enforce private connectivity. Finally, you will learn to interpret estimated costs shown during configuration and compare provisioned vCores against a serverless model for example workloads. Practically, this means you will open the portal, explore the 'Configure database' options, adjust vCore counts and storage, and observe cost estimates — then reflect on whether the selected tier meets availability and performance needs. This competency reduces surprises when you create production resources and helps you make decisions that align performance with budget.

Choosing between Platform as a Service and Infrastructure as a Service is a foundational planning decision. Platform as a Service, which includes Azure S Q L Database, Managed Instance, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL, hands off operating system management, patching, and much of the high availability work to the provider. This reduces operational burden and accelerates application delivery. In contrast, Infrastructure as a Service — a database running on an Azure Virtual Machine — gives you control over the OS, exact S Q L Server version, and all S Q L configuration, but that control comes with responsibility for patching, backups, and implementing high availability. A common concrete example: if you have legacy S Q L Agent jobs or cross-database queries that depend on specific S Q L Server features, IaaS or Managed Instance may be required because Azure S Q L Database may not expose every on-premises feature. A typical misconception is to assume PaaS means loss of control; instead, PaaS trades low-level control for managed capability, often improving reliability and reducing cost of operations. When deciding, list requirements for feature compatibility, control over OS, and acceptable operational overhead. Ask: do I need full engine control, or will managed platform features and built-in HA outweigh the benefits of control?

Azure S Q L Database exposes distinct service tiers to fit varying workload needs. General Purpose is intended for most business workloads; it balances performance and cost by decoupling compute and storage so you can scale resources independently. Business Critical is for input and output-intensive or mission-critical applications: it uses local SSD storage and multiple replicas to provide higher resilience and lower read latency. Hyperscale is an architecture that separates compute from storage differently and can scale to support very large databases by expanding storage independently and adding rapid scale-out techniques, making it suitable for massive OLTP scenarios. Each tier impacts latency, failover behavior, and cost. For instance, an OLTP workload with frequent small transactions might benefit from Business Critical for its local SSD performance, while an analytics-heavy or very large transactional dataset may require Hyperscale for growth beyond traditional limits. A common misconception is that higher tiers always fix application-level bottlenecks; tier selection addresses infrastructure capability, but poorly optimized queries or indexes will still limit performance. When choosing a tier, profile your workload's input and output patterns, size growth expectations, and tolerance for failover behavior, then map those needs to the tier characteristics.

Compute models determine how you size and pay for database resources. The vCore model exposes C P U and memory directly, allowing granular scaling of vCores and offering a provisioned or serverless option in some services. Provisioned vCores charge for allocated capacity regardless of use; this is predictable and useful for steady, high-utilization workloads. Serverless vCore lets compute scale with demand and can pause during inactivity to reduce cost, which is helpful for bursty or sporadic workloads. The DTU model, by contrast, packs compute, memory, and input and output into a single unit which simplifies sizing but reduces granularity. A concrete example: choosing provisioned vCores for a database with 24/7 steady traffic avoids repeated scaling events and gives predictable performance, while serverless may save money for a dev/test database that is idle many hours per day. The common misconception is that serverless always saves money; if a workload stays busy or requires consistent performance, serverless may be more expensive. When planning, compare usage patterns, the need for predictable latency, and cost estimates for each model to choose the right approach.

Azure S Q L Managed Instance is designed for enterprises looking to lift and shift on-premises S Q L Server workloads to a managed platform while retaining most on-premises features. It offers near 100% compatibility with the latest on-premises S Q L Server, making it a strong choice when migration requires features like S Q L Agent, cross-database queries, or specific configurations that Azure S Q L Database may not support. Managed Instance runs in your Virtual Network, enabling private connectivity that aligns with enterprise network topologies. Use cases include migrating applications with numerous cross-database dependencies or those that rely on OS-level collations and instance-scoped configurations. A common misconception is that Managed Instance removes all operational work; while it relieves you of OS patching and many management tasks, you still need to manage backups, schema migrations, and performance tuning. When planning a migration, inventory features in use, test application behavior against a Managed Instance, and plan VNet sizing and subnet allocation since Managed Instance requires VNet integration. The closing question is: which on-premises features are mandatory for your application, and does Managed Instance meet that compatibility checklist?

When using Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL, you will choose between Single Server and Flexible Server deployment models. Single Server is a fully managed PaaS offering that suits many workloads but has limitations in network isolation and high availability customization. Flexible Server provides more granular control over networking with VNet integration, zone-redundant high availability options, and a more predictable performance model. For production workloads requiring strict network isolation or zone-redundant availability, Flexible Server is the recommended path. A concrete scenario: if your application requires the database to be reachable only within a private VNet and you need zone redundancy, Flexible Server supports VNet integration and zone-redundant deployment, whereas Single Server may leave you constrained. A misconception is to assume Single Server is always simpler for production; while simpler in some respects, its network and HA constraints can make it less suitable for enterprise production needs. When planning, choose Flexible Server for new production deployments and use Single Server for simpler workloads or migration phases where its constraints are acceptable. Cost optimization should be considered at every planning step. Different service tiers and compute models have distinct pricing behaviors. For example, Business Critical tiers and provisioned vCores typically cost more than General Purpose or serverless because they allocate higher input and output or reserved compute. The Azure Hybrid Benefit is a licensing option that lets you use existing S Q L Server licenses to reduce cost, and reserved instances allow you to commit to one- or three-year terms to get lower prices for predictable workloads. A concrete scenario: if your workload is steady and predictable for enterprise databases, buying reserved capacity and using existing licenses through the Hybrid Benefit reduces ongoing bills. Conversely, if your workload is spiky or development-focused, serverless or Burstable tiers can reduce cost by charging only when resources are used. A misconception is to optimize only list price; instead, consider total cost of ownership including operations, monitoring, and maintenance. These key concepts summarize the chapter and should guide your deployment planning. First, PaaS versus IaaS is a trade-off between operational responsibility and control: PaaS reduces management overhead while IaaS gives full control of the OS and engine. Second, service tiers and compute models determine performance and pricing — General Purpose, Business Critical, and Hyperscale address different scale and resilience needs, while vCore, serverless, and DTU models change scaling behavior and cost. Third, secure networking is critical: use Virtual Networks, reserve subnet capacity, and prefer Private Endpoints when you must remove public exposure.
